schema.serviceName: Workflow automation for freelancers, consultants and small agencies
schema.serviceType: Business process automation and tool integration

hero.title: Workflow automation for freelancers: less admin, more time for real work.
hero.subtitle: I connect the tools you already use and remove the manual steps between leads, clients, email, proposals and reports. We start with one workflow. Just one.
hero.microcopy: No 40-page audit. No slides. One real workflow.
hero.emailSubject: Freelancer automation: the workflow I want to fix
hero.visualTitle: One workflow, not an endless project

problem.title: If you type the same data twice, the problem isn't you. It's the process.
paragraphs: You don't lack work. You lack time. More clients means more hours of copy-paste, reminders and spreadsheets only you understand.
symptoms: You copy the same contact into three places.
You rebuild the same report every month, from scratch.
You chase follow-ups instead of working.
problem.chaosCaption: Every tool works. You're the cable in between.

automations.title: Where time usually leaks
automations.intro: I start from what you do every week. Technology comes later.

cards.title: Leads and enquiries
cards.change: Enquiries arrive sorted. You just decide what to reply.

cards.title: Client onboarding
cards.change: The client gets the right questions. You stop forgetting step four.

cards.title: Follow-ups
cards.change: It tells you who to chase, with the history in front of you. You write the message.

cards.title: Proposals and reports
cards.change: Type it once, find it in the proposal and the report.

cards.title: Operations
cards.change: You keep your tools. What moves between them changes.

method.title: Small, testable. Then we'll see.
method.intro: Understand the problem first. Then decide whether to build.

steps.title: Find the bottleneck
steps.text: One call. Which workflow eats the most hours?

steps.title: Map it
steps.text: Who touches what, where it's duplicated, where it breaks.

steps.title: Build one small piece

steps.title: Check it helps
steps.text: In your real work, not in a demo.

steps.title: Grow it only if it works
steps.text: If it doesn't hold up, we say so and stop.

notes: If it's not worth it, I'll tell you.

example.aiTitle: AI: where it helps and where it doesn't

aiCannot.title: You decide
items: what goes out in your name.

fit.title: Not for everyone. Better to say it now.
forItems: You have a workflow that repeats every week.
You already use some tools, even if they don't talk.
You want to fix the process, not just hide it.
notForItems: You want a chatbot on your site and that's it.
You want to "do AI" without knowing what for.
You want a huge project without a clear problem.
fit.crossLinkText: Got a warehouse or a production floor?

credibility.title: No consultant talk
paragraphs: I've seen too many elegant solutions nobody uses. I built a couple of them myself.
Full stack developer, Computer Engineering student (intelligent systems), past life in a small software company with few resources and lots of fires. I use AI to work better, not to skip the skills.
principles: A good automation keeps working when I'm not around.

items.question: Where do we start?
items.answer: With a workflow you repeat often and hate. We look at it on a call and decide if it's worth it.

items.question: Do I have to change the tools I use?
items.answer: Rarely. I work on what moves between tools. If a tool is the problem, I'll tell you.

items.question: Can we automate without AI?
items.answer: Yes, and it's often better. Clear rules and integrations solve more than you'd think.

items.question: Will AI make decisions for me?
items.answer: No. It drafts and tidies up. Decisions stay with you.

items.question: How structured does my process need to be?
items.answer: Not perfect, it just has to exist. If it only lives in your head, we write it down together.

items.question: What does the free pilot include?
items.answer: {slots} spots until {deadline}. I map one workflow, propose a change and, if it makes sense, build a first automation. It's not a full project for free. In return I share the journey as a case study, only with what you approve.

items.question: What happens after the pilot?
items.answer: Your call. We continue with a clear quote, or I hand everything over so you can run it yourself. No obligation.

items.question: Do you only work with Italian freelancers?
items.answer: No. I work remotely, in English or Italian.

finalCta.title: Have a recurring workflow that steals time every week? Let's see whether it is worth automating.
finalCta.text: One call. If it's not worth it, I'll tell you. Costs me a client, saves you money.

problem.eyebrow: When the process only holds because people compensate
problem.title: If your process lives in spreadsheets, chats and people's memory, it isn't a process. It's a dependency.
problem.intro: Work keeps moving because people compensate. They aren't the problem: the system using them as a bridge is.

frictions.title: Always having to ask someone

problem.closing: Small frictions. Every day. They turn into delays and rework.

cards.title: Visible status and exceptions

build.iotNote: I don't sell hardware by the kilo. I only suggest it when a physical data point is missing and there's no simpler way.

constraint.eyebrow: From the floor to the software
constraint.title: Constraints first, technology second
paragraphs: I also work in logistics. You can't judge a workflow from a dashboard: it has to survive shifts, rush orders, absences and exceptions.
And I come from a software company where maintenance and thin resources were normal. I design for whoever uses the tool at 6 a.m. and whoever maintains it two years from now.
points: If it slows operators down, nobody will use it.
Every exception handled by word of mouth is lost data.
Fewer moving parts beat one more feature.

method.title: Six steps. Stopping is an option too.

steps.title: Site visit or call
steps.text: I look at the real process, not the one in the procedure.

steps.title: One pain point
steps.text: The one with the most errors, waiting or repeated questions.

steps.title: Prototype
steps.text: Small, testable, connected to real systems where possible.

steps.title: Field test
steps.text: Operators try it. Their opinion beats mine.

method.stopNote: Stopping after a pilot costs less than stopping after a project.

ai.title: AI doesn't fix a broken process
ai.statement: First clear data, responsibilities and handoffs. Then AI, only where it removes real work.
uses: Extracting data from orders, delivery notes, certificates.
Searching internal docs, with the source.
guardrails: A person checks before it becomes a decision.
We decide together which data leaves the company. If needed, models run locally.

fit.title: You need a problem, not a trend
forItems: You have a concrete operational problem that keeps coming back.
Someone can explain how it really works.
You're willing to try a small pilot.
notForItems: You want to replace every system in a week.
You want "an AI solution" to show off.
You want to buy technology before understanding the problem.

credibility.title: I write software, but I know the warehouse
paragraphs: Timings, handoffs, information that never arrives: I've seen them live, not on a slide.

Full stack developer (Python, Flask, Quart, Docker in production), n8n and Node-RED for automation, Computer Engineering student. I've also written about a Flask app born from real warehouse problems.
principles: Understand the problem first. Then decide whether to build.
A good automation keeps working when I'm not around.

items.question: Do we need to replace our ERP, WMS or MES?
items.answer: No. I work next to them: connecting, collecting data, adding what's missing.

items.question: Can we start with a single process?
items.answer: Yes, that's the right way. One workflow, one result you can check.

items.question: Do we need clean data first?
items.answer: No, but we need to know where it is. Often the first job is cleaning it.

items.question: Is AI required?
items.answer: No. Integrations, rules and alerts are often enough.

items.question: Can you work with Excel, email and our existing software?
items.answer: Yes, that's the most common case. We start there.

items.question: Do you do hardware and IoT as well?
items.answer: Yes, when needed: Arduino, ESP32, sensors. Only if there's no simpler way.

items.question: How do you handle data and access?
items.answer: Only the access needed, agreed in writing and documented. We decide together which data can leave. Any compliance requirements are checked with you before we start.

items.question: What does the free pilot include?
items.answer: {slots} spots until {deadline}. Mapping one workflow, a proposed change and, if it makes sense, a first integration. It's not a full project for free. In return I share the journey as a case study, only with what you approve.

items.question: How long does a first test take?
items.answer: Depends on the workflow and access. The goal is something to try within a few weeks. A precise estimate comes after the mapping.

items.question: What happens after the pilot?
items.answer: You decide: extend with a clear quote, adjust, or stop. No commitment.

finalCta.title: Is one recurring handoff slowing your operations every day? Let's map it and decide whether automation is worth it.
finalCta.text: Call or site visit. If it's not worth it, I'll tell you. Yes, I know it's a terrible sales technique.
